Kids and the top 1%: how the numbers were built

A guide to the SCF microdata, the sample, and every estimate in blog_post_text.md

Author

Mike Konczal

Published

October 16, 2026

What this is

This document explains, from the ground up, how the children-by-income numbers in blog_post_text.md were produced: what the Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) is, where its files live, the quirks of working with its microdata, how the sample and the children count are defined, how standard errors are computed, and which script produces which chart. Numbers below are pulled from graphics/post_numbers.csv (built 2026-10-15 21:43 EDT) and the output/ files.

1 The SCF in one page

The Survey of Consumer Finances is a household survey run by the Federal Reserve Board every three years. It is the main source for the distribution of US household wealth. The modern, comparable series starts in 1989, so there are 13 waves through 2025. Each wave interviews roughly 3,000 to 6,500 families about their balance sheets (assets and debts), their income, and their demographics.

Three features of its design matter for this project.

It oversamples the rich, on purpose. The SCF uses two samples. One is a standard area-probability sample of US households. The other is a “list sample” drawn from IRS Statistics of Income tax records, which heavily oversamples high-income and high-wealth families. People on the Forbes 400 list are excluded. Weights bring the combined sample back to the population. This is why the SCF can say something about the top 1%: a standard household survey of a few thousand families would have a few dozen of them at most.

“Family” and “head” have specific meanings. The unit is the primary economic unit (PEU): the core individual or couple who own or rent the home, plus everyone financially dependent on them. It is almost always the same as the household. The Fed labels one person the “reference person,” and calls them the “head” in its publications. The 2025 codebook defines the reference person as the single core individual in a PEU without a core couple, and in a couple as “the male in a mixed-sex couple or the older individual in the case of a same-sex couple.” When this document says “head aged 45-64,” it means that person’s age.

Timing. Balance-sheet questions refer to the interview date. Income questions refer to the previous calendar year: the 2025 survey asks about 2024 income.

2 Where the data live

Everything is published at the Fed’s SCF page, https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm. There is no login or API key. Each wave has its own page with download links; the file names follow fixed patterns, so they can be pulled directly from https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/. This project uses three kinds of files.

File What it is Fed file name (2025 example) Where it lives here Used for
Summary extract About 350 cleaned, Fed-constructed variables per family (net worth, income, KIDS, age, marital status, race, education…) in a consistent format across waves. Dollar values are restated in 2025 dollars for every wave. scfp2025excel.zip (one CSV inside, despite the name) data_raw/zips/, unzipped to data_raw/xlsx/SCFP{YEAR}.csv Income, net worth, age, children at home, weights, stock holdings
Full public data set Every question as asked, about 5,000+ raw variables named X1, X5910, etc. Dollar values are nominal. scf2025s.zip (Stata .dta inside); older waves are scf89s.zip … scf2016s.zip data_raw/full/p{YY}i6.dta (1992 is p92i4.dta) Children living elsewhere (X5910), prior marriages, work status and hours, wage income
Replicate weights 999 bootstrap replicate weights for computing sampling standard errors. scf2025rw1s.zip data_raw/rw/p{YY}_rw1.dta (1989-1998 and 2013-2025) Standard errors on the headline gaps

The codebook for each wave documents every X variable: exact question wording, codes, and disclosure edits. It is a plain-text file at https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk{YEAR}.txt. Copies for 2013, 2019, 2022 and 2025 are in docs/. To look up a variable, search the codebook for its name at the start of a line, for example grep -n "^X5910" docs/codebk2025.txt.

The full-data files are large (about 0.2-0.3 GB each as .dta, 2.9 GB for all 13 waves). R/01_download.R fetches only the summary extracts. The full-data and replicate-weight files were downloaded by hand. To fetch them from scratch (run from the project root):

# Full public data, all 13 waves (1989-1998 use two-digit years in the file name)
mkdir -p data_raw/full data_raw/rw output
for y in 89 92 95 98 01; do curl -fsL -o data_raw/full/scf${y}s.zip https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf${y}s.zip; done
for y in 2004 2007 2010 2013 2016 2019 2022 2025; do curl -fsL -o data_raw/full/scf${y}s.zip https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf${y}s.zip; done
# Replicate weights: the five pooled waves used in the significance tests, plus 1989-1998 for the period test (R/27)
for y in 2013 2016 2019 2022 2025; do curl -fsL -o data_raw/rw/scf${y}rw1s.zip https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf${y}rw1s.zip; done
for y in 89 92 95 98; do curl -fsL -o data_raw/rw/scf${y}rw1s.zip https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf${y}rw1s.zip; done
# Unzip in place
for f in data_raw/full/*.zip; do unzip -o "$f" -d data_raw/full; done
for f in data_raw/rw/*.zip; do unzip -o "$f" -d data_raw/rw; done

3 Five things that trip up new SCF users

3.1 Every family appears five times (multiple imputation)

When respondents skip a question or answer with a range, the Fed fills in the missing value by statistical imputation. Rather than release one guess, it releases five complete copies of the data set (“implicates”), each with a different random draw for the imputed values. So a file with 4,360 families has 21,800 rows.

Two ID variables tie this together: YY1 is the family’s case number and Y1 = 10 × YY1 + implicate number (1 to 5). Here is one 2025 family across its five implicates. Age and the number of children at home were answered and are the same in every row; net worth and income contain imputed components and differ.

Show code 
sx <- readRDS("data/scf_linked.rds")
ex <- sx[year == 2025, if (uniqueN(NETWORTH) == 5 && uniqueN(INCOME) > 1) .SD, by = YY1][YY1 == min(YY1)]
ex[, .(year, YY1, Y1, implicate, AGE, KIDS, NETWORTH = round(NETWORTH), INCOME = round(INCOME), WGT = round(WGT))]
    year   YY1    Y1 implicate   AGE  KIDS NETWORTH INCOME   WGT
   <num> <int> <int>     <int> <int> <int>    <num>  <num> <num>
1:  2025     2    21         1    69     1  3005160  66757 13728
2:  2025     2    22         2    69     1  2988260  65730 14391
3:  2025     2    23         3    69     1  2984260  66757 13047
4:  2025     2    24         4    69     1  2992170  65730 14897
5:  2025     2    25         5    69     1  3016280  67784 16109

The weight also differs slightly across implicates, because the Fed computes it separately for each one. That is another reason to always carry WGT row by row rather than attaching one weight per family.

The project’s convention (in R/scf_functions.R) is to compute point estimates on the pooled file: all five implicates stacked, each weighted. For means this is very close to, but not exactly the same as, averaging the five implicate-level estimates: weights, and for subgroups such as income bins group membership, differ slightly across implicates. For the 3+ shares by income bin the difference is under 0.01 points. The spread across implicates is imputation uncertainty, and it enters the standard errors (section 6).

3.2 Weights are essential, and the extract’s weight is pre-divided by 5

Because of the oversample, unweighted SCF statistics are meaningless for population questions. In the summary extract the weight WGT is already divided by 5, so summing it over all rows of a wave (all five implicates) gives the number of US families. The full data set’s weight, X42001, is not divided by 5. This project always uses WGT from the extract.

Show code 
sx[, .(sample_families = uniqueN(YY1), rows = .N, us_families_millions = round(sum(WGT) / 1e6, 1)), by = year][order(year)]
Key: <year>
     year sample_families  rows us_families_millions
    <num>           <int> <int>                <num>
 1:  1989            3143 15715                 93.0
 2:  1992            3906 19530                 95.9
 3:  1995            4299 21495                 99.0
 4:  1998            4305 21525                102.5
 5:  2001            4442 22210                106.5
 6:  2004            4519 22595                112.1
 7:  2007            4417 22085                116.1

10:  2016            6248 31240                126.0
11:  2019            5777 28885                128.6
12:  2022            4595 22975                131.3

The oversample is visible in our own analysis sample. Pooling 2013-2025, families in the top 1% of income (for their age) are 1390 of the 11,215 families in the sample, or 12% of the unweighted cases, though they represent 1% of families once weighted. That is what makes a top-1% estimate possible at all.

3.3 Dollar units differ between the two data sets

The summary extract restates every wave in the dollars of the newest survey (2025 dollars, deflated by the Fed with CPI-U-RS). The full public data are in nominal dollars. In this project all dollar amounts used in comparisons come from the extract (INCOME, NORMINC, NETWORTH, EQUITY). From the full data we take only counts (children), codes (marital history, work status), hours, and wages used within a single wave (ranks and ratios), where nominal units do not matter.

3.4 Unasked questions are often coded 0, not missing

Many codebook entries use 0 for “Inap.” (inapplicable: the question was skipped for this family) and negative codes for special answers. X5910 codes “None” as -1. Always read the codebook entry before using a raw variable. R/07_kids_income.R converts X5910 with pmax(x5910, 0) so that “None” becomes 0.

Show code 
# Raw coding of X5910 in the 2025 full public file, before any recoding (implicate 1 only)
f25 <- as.data.table(zap_labels(read_dta("data_raw/full/p25i6.dta", col_select = c(y1, x5910))))
f25[y1 %% 10 == 1, .N, by = .(x5910)][order(x5910)]

3.5 The public file is not the Fed’s internal file

To protect respondents, the public data are altered before release: some values are top-coded (X5910 at 10), rounded, or perturbed, and some variables are withheld. Published Fed tables use the internal data, so public-file estimates can differ slightly, especially means of skewed variables at the very top.

4 Building the analysis file

The pipeline joins the summary extract to the full public data, family-implicate by family-implicate, on Y1.

R/01_download.R  -> data_raw/xlsx/SCFP{YEAR}.csv           summary extracts, 13 waves
R/02_build_db.R  -> data/scf_linked.rds                    extracts stacked: 312,540 family-implicate rows
R/07_kids_income.R  -> output/kids_main.rds                adds X5910 etc. from data_raw/full/*.dta, builds the sample
R/24_kids_blended.R -> output/kids_blended.rds             remarried-couple robustness
R/25_rep_inference.R -> output/kids_rep5.rds              significance tests, pooled 2013-2025
R/26_top1_definitions.R -> output/kids_top1_defs.rds     robustness to the top-1% definition; definitions.html
R/27_period_change_test.R -> output/kids_period_change.rds  1989-1998 vs. 2013-2025 change, replicate weights
R/28_bin_intervals.R -> output/kids_bin_ci.rds              replicate-weight bands for the income and wealth charts
R/29_family_count_checks.R -> output/kids_count_checks.rds  double-count and marriage-history checks (footnote 2)
R/23_kids_wealth_work.R -> output/kids_wealth_work.rds     work hours within the top 1% by wealth
R/22_post_kids_graphics.R -> graphics/*.png, graphics/post_numbers.csv

R/02_build_db.R reads the 13 extract CSVs and stacks them into one table, scf_linked.rds. It renames the 1989 IDs (X1/XX1) to Y1/YY1, computes implicate, and checks that every wave has implicates 1-5 with equal rows and no duplicate IDs. It stops with an error if any check fails. Its one edit to the Fed’s values: the usual-income category variables are blanked in 1989 and 1992, because the usual-income dollar amount was not collected in those waves. It is a pooled cross-section, not a panel. Case 1001 in 2019 and case 1001 in 2022 are different families.

R/07_kids_income.R reads a handful of raw variables from each wave’s full file (handling the 1989 file’s uppercase names and X1 ID), merges them onto the extract by year and Y1, and checks that no rows are lost in the merge. It then defines everything below.

5 Definitions

5.1 Children

\[ \text{kids} \;=\; \underbrace{\texttt{KIDS}}_{\text{children living at home}} \;+\; \underbrace{\max(\texttt{X5910},\,0)}_{\text{children living elsewhere}} \]

  • KIDS (summary extract): the number of household-roster members coded as a child of the reference person or spouse/partner. In the public file that roster code (4) is labeled “CHILD (in-law)”, so KIDS also counts children-in-law living in the household. The roster also lists financially dependent children who do not usually live there (for example, college students), and they are counted too.
  • X5910 (full data, asked in every wave since 1989): “Altogether, including children from previous marriages and adopted children, how many sons and daughters do you (or your spouse/partner) have who do not live with you?” Interviewers are told to include only living children and stepchildren. It is top-coded at 10 in the recent public files; three families in the 1989 and 1992 files report more (up to 16), which cannot change the 3+ share and barely moves the early-period means.

The SCF never asks “how many children have you ever had.” The sum above is the closest available measure. It counts adopted children and stepchildren, it counts children-in-law at home, and it misses children who have died. It is a count of children associated with the current family, not of births to one person.

Possible double count. A dependent child who is on the roster but away from home (relationship code 4, with residence code 5, “does not usually live here”) can be reported again in X5910 as a child who does not live with the respondent. About 2.4% of top-1% families have both a roster-away child and X5910 > 0. R/29_family_count_checks.R subtracts the maximum possible overlap, the smaller of those two counts, either from both groups or only from the top 1%. Both rankings retain positive, statistically significant gaps under these specified overlap corrections; the full table is in the counting-checks section below. These scenarios address possible duplication captured by the residence flags, not all child-count measurement error.

5.2 Sample: families with a head aged 45 to 64

Restricting to heads aged 45-64 means most families have finished having children and most children have not yet died. The count is still a family child count, not completed fertility (see above). The age is the reference person’s, which in a mixed-sex couple is the man’s, so a younger partner may still have children. The older-family check in R/29_family_count_checks.R, restricting to heads aged 50-64 with a partner aged at least 45 when present, also finds significant income and wealth gaps. The trade-off is that income and wealth are measured after the children arrive (section 8).

5.3 Income and wealth ranks

  • Income measure. NORMINC, the family’s “usual” income: respondents are asked whether last year’s income was unusually high or low, and if so, what it would have been in a normal year. Using it keeps a one-off capital gain or a bad year from moving a family into or out of the top 1%. The usual-income dollar amount behind NORMINC was not collected in 1989 and 1992 (1992 asks only whether income was unusually high or low, X7650), so those waves use actual INCOME. Both include all sources: wages, business income, interest, dividends, capital gains, rents, transfers.
  • Ranking within age band. Each family gets a weighted percentile rank (the midpoint of its cumulative weight) among families in the same survey year, implicate, and 5-year age band of the head (45-49, 50-54, 55-59, 60-64). This compares families at the same stage of life: a 62-year-old near retirement is ranked against other 60-64-year-olds, not against 50-year-olds at peak earnings. Net worth (NETWORTH) is ranked the same way.
  • Bins. Ten deciles, with the top decile split into 90th-95th, 95th-99th and the top 1%.
  • Dollar labels on the charts. The x-axis labels show the income at each percentile cutoff among all heads 45-64 (pooled 2013-2025, 2025 dollars). Because the ranks are within age band and survey year, these are approximate: 58-87% of each bin’s families fall inside its labeled range, best at the top. The top-1% cutoff is about $1.4 million of usual income; the median top-1% family has about $2.1 million.

5.4 Pooling waves

The 2025 wave has only 208 top-1% families in this age range, too few for stable estimates. The main estimates pool the five most recent surveys, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025. The over-time chart uses three periods: 1989-1998, 2001-2010 and 2013-2025.

Within a period each wave gets equal total weight (w = WGT / sum(WGT) within each year and implicate). Without this, later waves would count for more simply because the population grew.

6 Estimation and standard errors

Point estimates. Weighted shares and means on the pooled implicates, using w.

Approximate standard errors (now used only for the married-couple bin numbers and the period regression table; the chart bands use replicate weights, below). For each implicate separately, a weighted regression of the outcome on bin dummies (fixest::feols, standard errors clustered on family, which within one implicate amounts to heteroskedasticity-robust errors). The five results are combined with Rubin’s rules:

\[ \bar{\theta} = \tfrac{1}{5}\textstyle\sum_m \hat{\theta}_m, \qquad T = \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{5}\textstyle\sum_m \widehat{V}_m}_{\text{within-implicate}} + \left(1+\tfrac{1}{5}\right)\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{4}\textstyle\sum_m (\hat{\theta}_m - \bar{\theta})^2}_{\text{between-implicate}}, \qquad \text{SE} = \sqrt{T}. \]

These ignore the SCF’s stratified sample design, so they are approximate.

Replicate-weight standard errors (the significance claims). The Fed’s replicate-weight file gives 999 alternative weights for each family, each mimicking a redraw of the sample. R/rep_se.R follows the Fed’s recipe:

  1. Compute the statistic on implicate 1 with each of the 999 replicate weights (replicate weight r = wt1br × mmr).
  2. Sampling variance \(V_s = \frac{1}{998}\sum_r (\hat{\theta}_r - \bar{\theta}_r)^2\).
  3. Add imputation variance: \(\text{SE} = \sqrt{V_s + 1.2\,B}\), where \(B\) is the variance of the statistic across the five implicates.

The headline significance tests (R/25_rep_inference.R) apply this recipe to all five pooled waves, 2013-2025, so they test the same estimates the charts show. Three details go beyond a single-wave calculation:

  • Pooled estimator. Each wave’s weights are scaled to sum to one, so every survey counts equally, as in the charts. A pooled share is a ratio of moments summed across waves, and the point estimates equal the charted levels.
  • Ranks re-estimated in every replicate. “Top 1%” is itself an estimated percentile. Each replicate recomputes the income (or wealth) ranks within age band before assigning families to groups; holding ranks fixed would ignore that uncertainty, and for the main comparisons here it gives smaller standard errors.
  • Independent waves. Each wave’s replicate variance is computed separately and combined through the derivative of the pooled ratio (delta method). The imputation term \(1.2B\) is computed on the pooled statistic across the five implicates.

Chart bands. R/28_bin_intervals.R applies the same recipe to every percentile bin on the income and wealth charts: replicate weights for all five waves, ranks re-estimated in each replicate (so uncertainty about which families fall in each bin is included), and imputation variance. Its top-1% values and SEs reproduce R/25 exactly. The bands are pointwise intervals for each bin, not tests of differences between bins.

Intervals are normal approximations. The five-wave estimates and standard errors in R/25 are cross-checked by audit/audit_checks.R. Single-wave replicate-weight results for 2019, 2022 and 2025 (R/rep_se.R, ranks held fixed) are included only to show wave-to-wave noise; they are not the headline inference.

7 Every chart and number in the post

7.1 Chart 1: who owns the stock market (2025)

All families in 2025 (not just ages 45-64), sorted by net worth. EQUITY from the extract is stock held directly and indirectly through mutual funds and retirement accounts. The bottom 50% by wealth own 1.1% of stock (SE 0.1); the wealthiest 10% own 81%. 56% of families own any stock. Ranking by stock holdings instead of wealth gives a top-10% share of 87%, which is why the post says “wealthiest 10%.” Standard errors use 2025 replicate weights.

7.2 Charts 2 and 3: children by income, 2013-2025

Income group 3+ children SE Average children SE
Bottom 10% 36% 1.5 2.23 0.06
40th-50th 41% 1.9 2.43 0.08
50th-60th 43% 2 2.49 0.08
80th-90th 37% 1.6 2.33 0.05
90th-95th 39% 2.6 2.29 0.07
95th-99th 41% 2.3 2.43 0.06
Top 1% 49% 3.3 2.51 0.08

Standard errors in the table are replicate-weight SEs for each bin (R/28_bin_intervals.R; percentage points and children), the same ones that draw the chart bands. The formal tests use replicate weights on the pooled 2013-2025 sample (R/25_rep_inference.R):

  • Top 1% vs. 90th-99th, share with 3+ children: +9.1 (SE 3.8; 95% CI 1.8 to 16.5) points; the 95% interval excludes zero.
  • Where the gap sits: 34% of the top 1% have exactly three children, against 24% of the 90th-99th (gap +9.9 (SE 3.5; 95% CI 3.1 to 16.7) points). Four or more: 15% vs. 16% (gap -0.8 (SE 2.6; 95% CI -5.8 to 4.3)). The excess is at the third child.
  • Top 1% vs. the middle (40th-60th): +6.9 (SE 3.5; 95% CI 0.0 to 13.7) points. The lower end of the interval is 0.05, borderline at best given the many comparisons examined, so the post compares the 1% with the affluent rather than with everyone.
  • Average children, top 1% vs. 90th-99th: +0.16 (SE 0.10; 95% CI -0.03 to 0.34); the 95% interval includes zero. The post reports the two averages without claiming a difference.

The pattern is not stable wave to wave: in 2025 alone the gap is +18 points (SE 9), in 2022 it is +4 (SE 8). Pooling is necessary.

Blended families. A natural worry is that rich men remarry and combine children from several relationships. The public SCF cannot identify stepchildren directly, but it does record whether each partner’s marriage was their first (X7377, X7392). R/24_kids_blended.R drops couples where either partner has been married more than once (code 2 on either question), keeping each family’s rank from the full sample. Those couples report more children on average (3.15 vs. 2.47 for first-marriage couples). Without them, the gap holds under both rankings in the five-wave replicate-weight tests: by income, +10.3 (SE 4.4; 95% CI 1.7 to 18.9) points; by wealth, +12.2 (SE 4.6; 95% CI 3.2 to 21.2) points. Among couples where both partners report a first marriage, the income gap is +12.6 (SE 4.8; 95% CI 3.2 to 22.0) points. The remarried flag is a proxy: the summary MARRIED flag includes cohabiting couples, so a divorced person married only once and now living with a new partner is not dropped, and it misses children from earlier non-marital relationships, so this rules out remarriage as the explanation, not every kind of blended family.

7.3 Charts 4 and 4b: has this changed over time?

Same sample and definitions, run separately for 1989-1998, 2001-2010 and 2013-2025, using all 13 waves. Chart 4, in the post, compares only the two endpoints, 1989-1998 and 2013-2025; chart 4b (not in the post) shows all three periods. Ranks are within each wave, so these charts use percentile labels, not dollars (real incomes at a given percentile differ across periods). The top 1% share with 3+ children is 49%, 48% and 49% across the three periods; the middle (50th-60th) goes from 50% to 43%.

A regression of 3+ children on a top-1% dummy, with age and year fixed effects, among the top 10% only, gives the top-1% gap relative to the 90th-99th in each period:

Period Gap (points) SE (approx.)
1989-1998 -3.7 4.9
2001-2010 +8.0 4.0
2013-2025 +9.0 3.7

The regression SEs above are approximate. R/27_period_change_test.R gives the design-based test of the change between 1989-1998 and 2013-2025, using the same estimator as R/25: replicate weights for all nine waves, ranks re-estimated in every replicate, each wave weighted equally within its period, independent waves, and imputation variance on the period difference itself. Its 2013-2025 gaps reproduce R/25 exactly. Because the early period mixes income measures (actual income in 1989 and 1992, when the usual-income amount was not collected), it also ranks by actual income in every wave, and by net worth.

Show code

lv <- function(z) sprintf("%.1f", z$est)
pt <- rbindlist(lapply(unique(pc$rank), function(r) { z <- pc[rank == r]; g <- function(pp, st) z[period == pp & stat == st]
  data.table(Ranking = r, `Top 1%, 1989-98` = lv(g("early", "top")), `Top 1%, 2013-25` = lv(g("recent", "top")),

             `Change in gap` = pf(g("change", "gap")), `p (gap)` = sprintf("%.3f", g("change", "gap")$p)) }))

actual income 52.1 49.7 -2.4 (-11.9 to 7.1) -14.4 (-20.5 to -8.4) +12.1 (0.5 to 23.6) 0.040
net worth 51.1 50.2 -0.9 (-10.0 to 8.2) -13.1 (-18.7 to -7.4) +12.1 (1.4 to 22.9) 0.027

Under all three rankings the gap widened significantly. That widening comes from the 90th-99th, whose 3+ share fell about 13 points; the top 1% share shows no detectable change, though its interval is wide (roughly plus or minus 10 points). Intervals are pointwise.

7.4 Charts 5 and 5b: ranking by wealth instead of income

Identical to charts 2 and 3, but families are ranked by net worth within age band. The top-1% wealth cutoff is about $17.1 million. The share with 3+ children peaks at 47% in the 20th-30th percentile (about $20,000 to $73,000), falls to 34% in the 70th-80th (about $640,000 to $1.1 million), then is 50% at the top 1%. Average children follow the same shape: 2.66, 2.14, and 2.52.

Replicate-weight tests on the pooled 2013-2025 sample, top 1% vs. 90th-99th by wealth: +12.9 (SE 3.8; 95% CI 5.5 to 20.4) points for the share with 3+ children (the 95% interval excludes zero), and +0.28 (SE 0.10; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.47) for average children. Excluding remarried couples: +12.2 (SE 4.6; 95% CI 3.2 to 21.2) points. The wealth result is at least as strong as the income one. An earlier three-wave test (2019-2025) made it look weaker because it left out 2013 and 2016, the waves with the largest wealth gaps.

7.5 Robustness: how the top 1% is defined

R/26_top1_definitions.R reruns the headline test (share with 3+ children, top group minus the rest of the top 10%) under different definitions of the top group. The outcome, sample (heads 45-64, 2013-2025) and inference are unchanged: 999 replicate weights per wave with ranks re-estimated in every replicate, plus imputation variance, as in R/25. For the pooled-across-years ranking, ranks depend on all five waves at once, so the variance is taken over replicate draws of the summed moments rather than summed wave by wave. The script checks that its baseline row reproduces R/25 exactly and also writes a standalone table, definitions.html.

Show code 
td <- readRDS("output/kids_top1_defs.rds")
fmt <- function(z) if (!nrow(z)) "n/a" else sprintf("%+.1f (%.1f to %.1f)%s", z$gap, z$lower, z$upper, if (z$lower > 0) "" else ", n.s.")
tab <- unique(td[, .(id, label)])
tab[, `Income gap, pts (95% CI)` := vapply(id, function(i) fmt(td[id == i & rank == "income"]), "")]
tab[, `Wealth gap, pts (95% CI)` := vapply(id, function(i) fmt(td[id == i & rank == "wealth"]), "")]
knitr::kable(tab[, -"id"], col.names = c("Definition", names(tab)[3:4]))
Definition Income gap, pts (95% CI) Wealth gap, pts (95% CI)
Current definition +9.1 (1.8 to 16.5) +12.9 (5.5 to 20.4)
Wider age bands +12.0 (4.5 to 19.5) +13.4 (7.0 to 19.8)
One ranking for all 45-64 +11.5 (4.4 to 18.6) +16.1 (9.4 to 22.9)
Whole population +8.8 (2.5 to 15.0) +10.8 (4.4 to 17.1)
Pooled across 2013-2025 +13.8 (6.5 to 21.0) +14.2 (7.1 to 21.3)
Actual income +10.6 (3.1 to 18.1) n/a
Top 2% +7.4 (1.4 to 13.5) +9.3 (2.6 to 16.0)
Top 0.5% +14.6 (6.3 to 23.0) +12.5 (5.2 to 19.8)

15 of 15 gaps have 95% intervals that exclude zero. The definitions select heavily overlapping families from the same surveys, so these are checks that the choice of definition is not driving the result, not independent confirmations. Intervals are pointwise and unadjusted for multiple comparisons.

7.6 Counting checks (footnote 2 of the post)

R/29_family_count_checks.R reruns the headline test (top 1% vs. 90th-99th, share with 3+ children) under the counting and family-history checks cited in the post’s second footnote. Ranks always come from the full sample, so each check changes only which families, or which children, enter the comparison. The overlap corrections subtract the largest possible double count, min(A, B), where A is roster children who do not usually live in the household (relationship code 4 with residence code 5) and B is X5910. “Currently married, first marriage” requires both partners to be currently married to each other (X8023 = 1, X105 = 1) and both to report a first marriage, so unlike R/24’s flag it excludes cohabiters. The older-family check keeps heads aged 50-64 whose spouse or partner, if present, is at least 45 (X19). The script checks that its baseline reproduces R/25 and that the separate checks reproduce the independent audit (audit/review_20261015/results/independent_inference.csv).

Show code 
cc <- readRDS("output/kids_count_checks.rds")
lab <- c(baseline = "Baseline", overlap_all = "Subtract maximum possible double count, all families",
         overlap_top = "Subtract it only in the top 1% (adverse case)", strict_first = "Currently married, both in a first marriage",
         older = "Head 50-64, partner (if any) 45+", strict_first_overlap_all = "First marriage + double-count correction, all families",
         strict_first_overlap_top = "First marriage + correction only in the top 1%")
cf <- function(z) sprintf("%+.1f (%.1f to %.1f)", z$gap, z$lower, z$upper)
ct <- data.table(Check = lab[unique(cc$spec)],
                 `Income gap, pts (95% CI)` = sapply(unique(cc$spec), function(s) cf(cc[rank == "inc_rank" & spec == s])),
                 `Wealth gap, pts (95% CI)` = sapply(unique(cc$spec), function(s) cf(cc[rank == "nw_rank" & spec == s])))
knitr::kable(ct)
Check Income gap, pts (95% CI) Wealth gap, pts (95% CI)
Baseline +9.1 (1.8 to 16.5) +12.9 (5.5 to 20.4)
Subtract maximum possible double count, all families +8.5 (1.0 to 15.9) +13.2 (5.5 to 20.8)
Subtract it only in the top 1% (adverse case) +7.8 (0.4 to 15.2) +12.3 (4.6 to 19.9)
Currently married, both in a first marriage +13.2 (3.9 to 22.6) +11.0 (1.6 to 20.4)
Head 50-64, partner (if any) 45+ +12.0 (3.9 to 20.2) +15.2 (7.7 to 22.7)
First marriage + double-count correction, all families +11.8 (2.4 to 21.3) +10.6 (0.9 to 20.4)
First marriage + correction only in the top 1% +11.4 (2.0 to 20.9) +9.9 (0.3 to 19.6)

All intervals exclude zero; the adverse combined wealth check only narrowly (lower bound 0.3). These checks address specific counting problems. They cannot identify births to one person or rule out every kind of blended family, for example children from earlier non-marital relationships.

7.7 Work hours within the top 1% by wealth

R/23_kids_wealth_work.R adds usual weekly hours on the main job for the head (X4110) and spouse/partner (X4710), summed, with 0 for those not working. Among families in the top 1% of wealth (pooled 2013-2025):

The difference (under 40 minus 40+ hours) is +0.9 points (SE 7.3), or +0.4 (SE 8.4) without remarried couples. Hours are measured at 45-64, long after most children were born.

8 Caveats

  • Reverse causation. Income, wealth and hours are measured when the head is 45-64, after the children. Children can lower family earnings (especially mothers’), which would push large families down the income ranks in the middle of the distribution more than at the top, where wages are a smaller share of income. The post treats the results as correlations.
  • Children count. Includes stepchildren, adopted children and children-in-law at home; excludes children who died; can double-count a dependent child away from home (see Definitions). “Remarried couple” is a proxy for possible stepchildren, not a direct measure: it misses children from earlier non-marital relationships. Never-married cohabiting partners count as not remarried, but they are excluded from the stricter “first-marriage couple” group, which requires both partners to report a first marriage. Cohabiting partners who were married once before report that marriage as their first, so they count as not remarried and can fall in the “first-marriage couple” group.
  • Family counts. Reported numbers of families count a family in a bin if it falls there in any implicate, so they slightly overstate per-implicate cell sizes. Estimates are unaffected.
  • Age-band ranks. “Top 1%” means top 1% among families whose head is the same age, in the same survey year. Dollar labels on charts are approximate. Other definitions of the top group give the same result (see the robustness section).
  • Public-data edits (top-coding, rounding, perturbation) mainly affect the very top.
  • Chart bands. Pointwise 95% intervals for each group, from replicate weights with ranks re-estimated (R/28_bin_intervals.R). Overlapping bands do not mean a gap is insignificant: the top 1% vs. 90th-99th gaps are tested directly (R/25_rep_inference.R).
  • Who is the head. In mixed-sex couples the reference person is the man, so “head aged 45-64” is the man’s age. For families where the woman is younger, her childbearing may be less complete.

9 Reproducing everything

Run from the project root. The first two steps only need rerunning if the raw data change.

mkdir -p data_raw/full data_raw/rw output   # before the hand downloads (section 2) and R/07
Rscript R/01_download.R            # summary extracts -> data_raw/xlsx/, writes data_raw/download_manifest.csv
Rscript R/02_build_db.R            # -> data/scf_linked.rds
Rscript R/07_kids_income.R         # -> output/kids_main.rds (needs data_raw/full/*.dta)
Rscript R/24_kids_blended.R        # -> output/kids_blended.rds (needs data_raw/rw/*.dta)
Rscript R/23_kids_wealth_work.R    # -> output/kids_wealth_work.rds
Rscript R/25_rep_inference.R       # -> output/kids_rep5.rds (needs data_raw/rw/*.dta, 2013-2025)
Rscript R/26_top1_definitions.R    # -> output/kids_top1_defs.rds, definitions.html
Rscript R/27_period_change_test.R  # -> output/kids_period_change.rds (needs data_raw/rw/*.dta, 1989-1998 too)
Rscript R/28_bin_intervals.R       # -> output/kids_bin_ci.rds (chart bands)
Rscript R/29_family_count_checks.R # -> output/kids_count_checks.rds (needs data_raw/full/*.dta)
Rscript R/22_post_kids_graphics.R  # -> graphics/*.png, graphics/post_numbers.csv
quarto render kids_methods.qmd     # this document

Order matters: 07 first; 24, 25 and 28 before 22 (22 reads their outputs); 26, 27 and 29 after 25 (they check their baselines against it); and everything before rendering this file. Checks that a run worked: 02 prints families per wave (about 4,360 sample families and 135 million US families in 2025); 07 prints the main sample size (25,576 families across 13 waves); 22 ends by reporting that it wrote 337 numbers to graphics/post_numbers.csv.

R packages: data.table, haven, fixest, ggplot2, scales, ragg, dplyr (for all_of when selecting columns from .dta files).
